title: Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` (indexed from 0). Decide whether deleting exactly one element from it can leave an array in which every value is strictly larger than the value just before it. Return `true` if some single deletion achieves this and `false` if none does.

An array that is already strictly increasing also gives `true`, since deleting any one element keeps it strictly increasing.
notes:
## Intuition

The brute force deletes each index in turn and rescans the rest, which is O(n²). A single pass is enough: walk the array and count the places where a value fails to beat the last kept value. A second such place means no single deletion can help. At the first one, `nums[i] <= nums[i - 1]`, one of those two values has to go, and the greedy choice is to keep whichever leaves the **smaller** last value, because a smaller tail is easier for the rest of the array to beat.

## Approach

1. Let `last` be the last value of the kept array, starting with `nums[0]`; `removed` counts deletions.
2. For each `i` from 1: if `nums[i] > last`, keep it and set `last = nums[i]`.
3. Otherwise a deletion is needed. Increase `removed`; if it passes 1, return `false`.
4. If `i === 1` or `nums[i] > nums[i - 2]`, delete `nums[i - 1]` instead, so `nums[i]` becomes `last`. Otherwise delete `nums[i]` and leave `last` unchanged.
5. Return `true` after the loop.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1,2,10,5,7]`. `last` goes 1, 2, 10. At `i = 3`, `5` does not beat `10`, so `removed = 1`. Since `5 > nums[1] = 2`, the `10` is the one deleted and `last = 5`. At `i = 4`, `7 > 5`, so `last = 7`. The loop ends with one deletion: `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over `nums`.
- Space: O(1): two counters, no copy of the array.

## Pitfalls

- "Strictly" means equal neighbours are a violation: compare with `>`, not `>=`.
- Neither fixed choice works: always deleting `nums[i]` fails on `[10,1,2,3]`, where the `10` must go, and always deleting `nums[i - 1]` fails on `[3,4,1,5]`, where the `1` must go.
- Compare with `last`, not `nums[i - 1]`: after deleting `nums[i]`, the next value has to beat `nums[i - 1]`.
- An array with no violation is still `true`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `last` | last value of the array we keep after the deletions so far |
| `removed` | number of deletions made |
| `i` | index of the value being checked |

narration.2: No element has been deleted yet.
narration.3: The first value is always kept and becomes the value to beat.
narration.5: Check every later value against the last kept one.
narration.6: Does this value strictly beat the last kept value?
narration.7: Yes: keep it, and it becomes the new value to beat.
narration.9: No: nums[i] or nums[i - 1] has to be deleted, so count one deletion.
narration.10: A second deletion would be needed...
narration.11: ...so no single deletion can fix the array.
narration.13: If nums[i] beats the value two places back (or there is none), delete nums[i - 1] and keep the smaller tail.
narration.14: nums[i] becomes the last kept value; otherwise nums[i] itself is the one deleted.
narration.18: At most one deletion was needed, so the answer is true.
